clinicalPearls: A rare, usually sporadic sclerosing dysplasia in which dense cortical hyperostosis appears to flow along the length of a bone
The radiographic hallmark is irregular, wavy cortical thickening likened to dripping candle wax down one side of a long bone
Lesions frequently follow a sclerotomal distribution, tending to affect one limb along the territory of a spinal sensory nerve
Presents with limb pain, stiffness, restricted joint movement, and sometimes limb-length discrepancy or deformity, often beginning in adulthood
Overlying soft-tissue changes such as fibrosis, contractures, oedema, and skin thickening can accompany the bony disease
Somatic mosaic mutations, notably in MAP2K1 and related pathway genes, have been implicated in the endosteal and soft-tissue components
Management is symptomatic, addressing pain and function, with orthopaedic surgery reserved for disabling deformity or contracture
reference.pathophysiology: Melorheostosis is characterised by localised, progressive hyperostosis affecting the cortex of long bones and adjacent soft tissues. It is generally sporadic and non-hereditary, and recent work has identified somatic mosaic mutations, including activating changes in MAP2K1 within the MAP-kinase pathway, in affected lesional tissue, with other genetic changes reported in the endosteal component. Enhanced local signalling drives excess bone formation confined to affected regions, often distributed along a sclerotome, producing the characteristic asymmetrical flowing cortical thickening. Associated fibrosis and contracture of surrounding soft tissue contribute to the pain and functional limitation.
additionalDifferentials: Osteopoikilosis and osteopathia striata (mixed sclerosing bone dystrophy)
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs demonstrating the characteristic flowing candle-wax cortical hyperostosis
CT to define the extent and cortical involvement
MRI to assess soft-tissue fibrosis, contracture, and marrow
Bone scintigraphy showing increased uptake in active lesions
Assessment of joint range, limb length, and function
Biopsy or genetic analysis of lesional tissue in atypical cases to exclude malignancy
redFlags: New rapidly enlarging mass or pain raising concern for a surface osteosarcoma
Progressive contracture or neurovascular compromise of a limb
Significant limb-length discrepancy or deformity in a growing child
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and slowly progressive with a normal lifespan, but it can cause chronic pain, joint contracture, and functional impairment; outcomes depend on lesion location and the degree of soft-tissue involvement.
pitfalls: Mistaking the flowing hyperostosis for an aggressive surface bone tumour and vice versa
Assuming the condition is purely osseous and overlooking disabling soft-tissue fibrosis and contracture
Expecting a hereditary pattern when the disorder is typically sporadic and mosaic
Undertaking extensive surgery that may be complicated by recurrence and poor soft-tissue healing
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
Peer-reviewed reviews of melorheostosis and its somatic mosaicism
management: Control the chronic bone and soft-tissue pain with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and other analgesics
Maintain joint range and limit contracture with physiotherapy and stretching
Consider bisphosphonates in selected patients for pain associated with active hyperostosis
Undertake surgery such as contracture release, deformity correction or excision of excess bone for functional limitation and limb-length discrepancy
Consider MEK-pathway-directed therapy as an emerging targeted approach given the somatic MAP2K1 mutations in lesional tissue
Biopsy or genetically analyse lesional tissue in atypical cases to exclude malignancy
Monitor limb length, deformity and function over the long term
